title: Who Really Invented the Pollution Tax?

source.title: A History of Pricing Pollution (Or, Why Pigouvian Taxes are not Necessarily Pigouvian)

intro.summary: Economists usually say that charging polluters a price comes straight from A.C. Pigou's 1920s theory of 'externalities', meaning costs pushed onto bystanders. Banzhaf's 2020 working paper checks that story against what the 1960s pioneers (Allen Kneese, Thomas Crocker, John Dales) actually wrote and cited, and against citation counts from JSTOR and Google Scholar. He finds they rarely mentioned Pigou and drew instead on American traditions about shared, open-access resources and the development of land and water; the 'Pigouvian' label only spread around 1970. Limits: this is one historian's interpretation in a paper that was not peer-reviewed, and others such as Medema argue that Pigou's theory was simply 'grafted' onto the field or passed on as an unwritten oral tradition. The supporting encyclopedia sources (s1, s2) carry quality warnings, and they record live disagreements this lesson only touches: whether social costs can be measured well enough to set the tax, Coase's view that harm is reciprocal and bargaining can sometimes work, the double-dividend debate, and ecological economists' criticism of the whole externality idea. Good follow-ups are positive externalities and subsidies, the Coase theorem, and the double-dividend debate.
background: A market is where buyers and sellers trade, and the price they settle on usually reflects only the costs and benefits to those two sides.
An externality is a cost or benefit that lands on someone outside the deal, like the smoke a factory sends over a neighbour's washing.
A 'Pigouvian tax' is a charge on a harmful activity, ideally equal to the harm it does to others, named after the Cambridge economist Arthur Cecil Pigou (1877–1959).
Cap-and-trade is the cousin of a pollution tax: the government caps total pollution and lets firms buy and sell permits to pollute.
intro.aha: The 'Pigouvian tax' on pollution was mostly not built from Pigou: its 1960s inventors barely cited him and borrowed instead from American ideas about overused shared resources like fisheries and groundwater, and Pigou's name was attached to their work later.

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: Textbooks tell a tidy story. Pigou explained in the 1920s that markets ignore harms like smoke, and suggested taxing them. Forty years later, economists dusted off his idea and applied it to river and air pollution. Banzhaf asks whether that story is true, because two things don't fit: a long silence between Pigou and the 1960s, and how seldom the 1960s writers mentioned him.
primer.quote: However, the historical literature has noted problems with this narrative, including a 30-year gap in discussions of such applications and few actual citations to Pigou.

primer.heading: The basic economics
primer.body: When a refrigerator factory pollutes for free, the price of a fridge covers labour and metal but not the damage downstream. So fridges look cheaper than they really are to society, and too many get made. If the firm had to pay that damage, it would charge more, make fewer fridges and pollute less. Charging a price per unit of pollution, either as a tax or as tradable permits, is how economists propose to close that gap.
primer.quote: If firms were required to pay the social costs of pollution, they would create less pollution but produce less of the product and charge a higher price.

primer.heading: What they did
primer.body: This is a history paper, not an experiment. Banzhaf read the key 1960s works on pollution pricing: Kneese's 'effluent charges' (a fee per unit of waste dumped into a river) and Crocker's and Dales's tradable pollution rights. He traced whom they cited and how they argued. He also counted how often 'Pigouvian tax' appeared in journals over time, and how often papers mentioned Kneese with or without Pigou.
primer.quote: Though today economists might naturally refer to such prices as "Pigouvian taxes," at the time they were known simply as "effluent charges" (e.g. Kneese 1964), without making a connection to Pigou.

primer.heading: What they found
primer.body: The pioneers had been trained in farm, land and water economics. Their worries were about shared resources that nobody owns, such as a river or the air, which everyone uses up, and about the gains from developing water and land at large scale. Kneese, Crocker and Dales cited Scott Gordon's work on fisheries and Coase far more than Pigou. The term 'Pigouvian tax' appeared only a dozen times in the 1960s and took off after Baumol and Oates used it in 1971. So the Pigou label was mostly attached afterwards.
primer.quote: This paper has argued that the early literature on pollution pricing was rooted in questions about common property resources and the increasing returns from developing natural resources.

primer.heading: Why it matters, and its limits
primer.body: How we tell a field's history shapes how we argue about its tools. If pollution pricing grew from thinking about shared resources, it is less about blaming a single polluter and more about managing something everyone draws on. The usual 'Pigou versus Coase' contest then misses part of the picture. But this is an interpretation built from citations and texts, in a paper that was not peer-reviewed. Other historians explain the silence differently, for example as an unwritten 'oral tradition' of Pigou's ideas.
primer.quote: This paper offers a simple explanation for this puzzle: Namely, pollution pricing is not (necessarily) Pigouvian.

concepts.title: The cost nobody at the till pays
concepts.idea: When producers don't pay for the harm their pollution does, their supply curve sits too low, so the market makes more of the good than is best for society.

predict.question: Back to $100 of harm per fridge. A free filter cuts the pollution, so each fridge now does only $40 of harm. Makers still pay nothing for that harm. How many fridges does the market now make?
options: Still 45,000 fridges
43,000 fridges
40,000 fridges
More than 45,000, because cleaner fridges are more attractive
why: Right. The market's point sits where buyers' value meets the makers' own cost. Makers pay none of the harm, so a smaller harm doesn't move that line. Output stays at 45,000.
43,000 is the new best amount: the true-cost line drops by $60 and meets buyers' value further right. But the market doesn't follow that line, because nobody pays the harm.
40,000 was the best amount when the harm was $100. The harm has changed, and anyway the market never lands on the best amount while the harm goes unpaid.
Buyers' value and makers' own cost are both unchanged. Only the harm to outsiders fell, and neither buyers nor makers feel that harm. So nothing pushes output up.

terms.means: A harm that a deal does to people outside it, which nobody in the deal pays for
The cost the maker actually pays: labour, materials, energy
The private cost plus the harm done to everyone else; the true cost to society
Value society loses because the wrong amount of a good is made

model.title: The fridge market, with and without counting pollution harm
model.note: Teaching model: straight-line demand and supply fitted to the OpenStax fridge table (source s3). Pollution harm is a fixed amount per fridge, and there are no other spillovers. The $100 of harm, $650 with 45,000 fridges, and $700 with 40,000 fridges come from that textbook example. Other harm values and all the loss figures are illustrative, not measured data.

outputs.label: Net loss from the extra fridges

steps.say: This is a market for fridges. Going across is how many are made each year. Going up is the price of one fridge.
The falling blue line shows what buyers will pay. The more fridges there are, the less the last buyer values one.
The rising line shows what makers need to cover their own bills for labour, metal and energy.
The dashed line adds the damage that factory pollution does to the neighbours. This slider sets that damage per fridge. Watch the dashed line lift.
Two crossings matter: where the market actually lands, and where society would want it to land.

explore.prompt: You set how much harm each fridge's pollution does. Read the gap between the two crossings, and the loss it causes.

goals.text: Make the market produce exactly 7,500 more fridges than the best amount
hints: Which thing pulls the dashed line away from the makers' own cost line?
Watch the 'Extra fridges made' box as you move the harm slider. Each step adds the same number of extra fridges.
At the textbook's $100 of harm the gap is 5,000 fridges. You need half as much gap again.

goals.text: Make the net loss from the extra fridges exactly four times what it is at the textbook's $100 of harm
hints: The loss is a triangle between the dashed line and buyers' value. How does a triangle's area change when its height and its width both grow?
Both the height (the harm) and the width (the extra fridges) grow in step with the harm slider.
If both sides grow by the same factor, the area grows by that factor squared. Which factor, squared, gives 4?

feedback.correct: The market's point is set by buyers' value and the makers' own cost. Harm that nobody pays never enters that crossing, so changing the harm moves only the best amount, not what the market makes.
feedback.incorrect: You probably assumed the market reacts to the harm. It doesn't: makers price only what they pay. While the harm goes unpaid, only the best-for-society point moves, and the market stays at 45,000.

steps.say: Start with no pollution at all. The two cost lines sit on top of each other, so the market's point and the best point are the same: 45,000 fridges at $650.
Now take the textbook's case: each fridge's pollution does $100 of harm to people who neither made nor bought it. A harm like that, which no one in the deal pays for, is a negative externality.
Makers still pay only their private cost, the lower solid line. Nothing they pay has changed, so the market still lands at 45,000 fridges at $650.
The dashed line is the social cost: the private cost plus the $100 of harm. It meets buyers' value at 40,000 fridges and $700. That is the best amount for society.
So the market makes 5,000 fridges too many. For each one, the true cost is higher than what a buyer values it at.
The value wasted on those extra fridges is called deadweight loss. In this model it is $250,000 a year.
Now triple the harm. The gap triples to 15,000 fridges, but the loss grows nine-fold, because the triangle gets both taller and wider.

understand.explanation: A firm's supply line shows only the costs the firm itself pays. If its pollution harms neighbours for free, the true cost of each fridge sits above that line by the amount of the harm. The market settles where buyers' value meets the lower line, the firm's own cost. That point lies to the right of where buyers' value meets the true cost, so too many fridges get made, and the bigger the harm, the bigger the overshoot. The OpenStax reading shows this with its fridge table: counting $100 of harm per fridge moves the outcome from 45,000 fridges at $650 to 40,000 at $700, and the Wikipedia article makes the same argument with steel. Two caveats: real lines are not straight, and the harm per unit is very hard to measure in practice, a point critics of corrective taxes stress.
understand.quote: In the case of pollution, at the market output, social costs of production exceed social benefits to consumers, and the market produces too much of the product.
understand.quote_where: Reading: Introduction to Externalities and Pollution, section 'Pollution as a Negative Externality' (OpenStax)

connect.caption: The first part restates the source: the private cost falls short of the social cost by the external cost, h (the dashed line sits h above the solid one). The second part is this model's rule, not the paper's. In the fridge table, both lines change by 1,000 fridges for every $10 of price, so a gap of h dollars pushes the market h ÷ 20 thousand fridges past the best amount, which is 50 extra fridges per dollar of harm.

concepts.recap: If makers don't pay for their pollution, their costs look too low, so the market makes more than society would want, and the overshoot grows with the harm.

activities.title: Reading the textbook's fridge table

steps.text: Look at the first three columns. At $650, buyers want 45,000 fridges, and makers who count only their own costs offer 45,000. The two match.
Now make firms count $100 of pollution harm per fridge. Making each fridge costs them more, so at every price they offer fewer. That is the fourth column: at $650 they would offer only 35,000.
Find the row where buyers' quantity equals the new supply column. At $700, buyers want 40,000 and makers offer 40,000.
Compare the two rows. Counting the harm raises the price and cuts output by 5,000 fridges, and less output means less pollution.

activities.takeaway: Those 5,000 fridges are made only because nobody pays for their pollution. The curves in the model are these rows drawn as lines.

concepts.title: A tax that makes the price tell the truth
concepts.idea: A per-unit tax equal to the harm per unit lifts the private supply curve onto the true-cost curve, so the market lands on the socially best quantity by itself.

predict.question: A new case: a regulator believes each fridge does $100 of pollution harm, but the real harm is only $50. It sets a $100 tax per fridge. What happens?
options: The market lands on the best amount, because any tax pushes it the right way
The market makes too few fridges, and the net loss is about as big as with no tax at all
The market still makes too many fridges, because the tax is not big enough
The market makes too few fridges, but there is no net loss because there is less pollution
why: A tax does push the right way at first. But the market lands on the best amount only when the tax matches the real harm, and here it is double.

Right. The lifted line sits $50 above the true cost, as far above as the untaxed line sat below. The market cuts too far by the same amount, so the loss matches. Check it: harm $50, then compare a $0 and a $100 tax.
That would hold if the tax were below the harm. Here it is above the real harm, so the lifted line sits above the true-cost line and the market cuts too far.
Less pollution is good only while each fridge is worth more to buyers than its full cost. The fridges cut past the best amount were worth more than they cost everyone, so losing them is a real loss.

terms.means: A tax on each unit of a harmful good, set equal to the harm each unit does to other people
Make a maker count a harm it used to push onto others as part of its own cost

model.title: The fridge market, now with a tax on each fridge
model.note: Teaching model: straight-line demand and supply fitted to the OpenStax fridge table (source s3). Pollution harm is a fixed amount per fridge with no other spillovers. The tax is a fixed amount per fridge paid by makers. In the model you can see the true harm; a real government has to estimate it. The $100 of harm, $650 with 45,000 fridges and $700 with 40,000 fridges come from that textbook example. Other harm and tax values, tax revenue and all loss figures are illustrative, not measured data.

outputs.label: Fridges above the best amount (minus means too few)
Net loss from making the wrong amount

steps.say: This is the same fridge market as before. You can see the buyers' value line, the makers' own cost line, and the dashed true-cost line that adds the pollution harm.
One thing is new: a tax slider. Makers now pay this amount on every fridge they sell. Watch the new line lift up.
The market now settles where the lifted line meets buyers' value. Keep an eye on where this point lands.

explore.prompt: Now you set the tax. First find the tax that fixes a bigger harm. Then test how forgiving the market is when the tax overshoots.

goals.text: Suppose the harm turns out bigger than first thought. Raise it, then set a tax that makes the market land exactly on the best amount for society.
hints: The market follows the lifted line. Which line should the lifted line match?
Make the solid tax line lie right on top of the dashed true-cost line.
The tax per fridge has to match one other slider exactly.

goals.text: Leave the harm where it starts. Find a tax that is too high, yet still leaves less than half the net loss you get with no tax at all.
hints: With no tax, the loss box reads $250,000. A tax above the harm makes the market cut too far, but by how much?
Push the tax past the harm one step at a time and watch the net loss climb.
The loss grows faster and faster as you overshoot. Stay only a few steps above the harm.

feedback.correct: Yes. The tax works only because it equals the harm. Set at double the real harm, it lifts the makers' cost line as far above the true cost as the untaxed line sat below it. So the market cuts too far, and the loss is just as large.
feedback.incorrect: You may have assumed that any tax helps, or that less pollution is always better. The remedy is exact: the lifted line must sit on the true-cost line. Overshoot it and the fridges you lose were worth more to buyers than their full cost to everyone, so that loss is real too.

steps.say: Start with no tax. Makers count only their own cost, so the market makes 45,000 fridges, but the best amount is 40,000. That leaves a $250,000 net loss.
Add a $50 tax on each fridge. The makers' cost line lifts by $50, and the market point slides left to 42,500 fridges. The loss falls to $62,500.

Raise the tax to $100, the same as the harm. The lifted line lands on the dashed true-cost line, the market point sits on the best point, and the loss is zero. A tax set equal to the harm per unit is a Pigouvian tax.
Nobody told buyers or makers how many fridges to make. The price now carries the harm, and their own choices did the rest. Buyers pay $700, and the government collects $4 million as a side effect.
Push the tax to $200, twice the harm. Now the market cuts too far, to 35,000 fridges, which is 5,000 too few. The loss jumps back to $250,000, as big as with no tax at all.

Keep the $200 tax, but suppose the harm really is $200. The same tax is now exactly right and the loss is zero. When the tax matches the real harm, makers internalize it: they count the harm as their own cost.

understand.explanation: Without a tax, makers ignore the harm their pollution does, so the market makes too many fridges. A tax as large as the harm per fridge lifts the makers' cost line by exactly that harm, right onto the true-cost line. The market then slides to the best amount without anyone ordering it to. Pigou argued for this in his 1920 Economics of Welfare, and the textbook fridge example (source s3) shows a $100 shift moving the market from $650 and 45,000 fridges to $700 and 40,000. The catch is the word 'equal': a tax that is too low leaves some loss, and a tax that is too high makes the market cut too far and creates a new loss. Real governments must estimate the harm. Critics such as Baumol argue this is extremely hard to measure, and lobbying can push the rate up or down.
understand.quote: To deal with over-production, Pigou recommends a tax placed on the offending producer. If the government can accurately gauge the social cost, the tax could equalize the marginal private cost and the marginal social cost.

equation.text: lands on the best amount when

connect.caption: This is the model's rule, not a formula from the sources. The left side is buyers' value. The right side is the makers' own cost plus the tax t (orange-linked to the tax slider). The market makes the quantity Q where the two are equal. The sources state the matching rule in words: the per-unit tax should equal the marginal external cost, which is the harm h per fridge in this model.

activities.prompt: The harm is $100 per fridge in all three cases. Only the tax changes. Compare where the market lands and the size of the net loss.

cases.label: Tax set at twice the harm

activities.takeaway: The fix only works if you know the harm. In the model you can read the harm off a slider, but a real government has to estimate it. Pigou himself admitted 'we seldom know enough', Baumol argued that measuring social cost is almost impossible, and lobbying can pull the rate away from the harm. A wrong guess in either direction leaves a loss.

concepts.recap: Tax each unit by exactly the harm it does, and buyers' and makers' own choices land on the best amount, but only if the harm is known.

concepts.title: Everybody's fish is nobody's fish
concepts.idea: When anyone can use a shared resource for free, users keep joining until the average catch just covers their cost, which drains the resource's value; an owner or a price on access would stop much earlier.

predict.question: The price of fish doubles, so every catch is now worth twice as much. The fishing ground stays free for all. Once the fleet settles again, how much value is left over after running costs?
options: About twice as much as before
Nothing again: more boats join until each one just covers its cost
Less than before, because fewer boats will bother to fish
A loss: boats end up spending more than the catch is worth
why: Tempting, because each fish is worth more. But under free access the extra profit is a signal that draws newcomers in, and they keep coming until it is gone.

Right. A higher price raises the catch per boat above the running cost, so more boats join. They stop only when the catch per boat again just covers the cost, and that leaves zero over. The fleet gets bigger, but the value is drained just the same.
A higher price makes fishing more attractive, not less. So the fleet grows. Fish do get scarcer, but that happens because more boats join, not fewer.
Boats stop joining once the next one would not cover its own cost. So in this model the fleet settles where the leftover is zero, not below it.

terms.means: Something many people use but nobody owns outright, like a fishing ground, a river or the air
Anyone may use the resource, free, and no one can turn a newcomer away
The value a resource yields after paying the costs of using it: what an owner could keep as profit

model.title: Boats, catch and costs on one shared fishing ground
model.note: Teaching model: total catch follows a simple hump-shaped rule (10N − 0.1N²). Every boat is identical, fish sell at a fixed price, and the fleet is shown at the point where it settles, not season by season. This is a textbook version of Scott Gordon's 1954 fishery argument, which Banzhaf describes but does not reproduce. All numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data.

controls.label: Charge per boat to fish here

outputs.label: Boats if fishing is free for all
Boats a single owner would run
Most that could be left over

steps.say: This curve is the total catch from one fishing ground as more boats arrive. It rises, flattens, then falls: crowded boats thin out the fish.
This straight line is what the whole fleet costs to run. The slider sets the cost of running one boat.
This slider adds a charge each boat pays to fish here. The dashed line is running costs plus that charge.
This slider puts a fleet of your chosen size on the water. The boxes show its catch and what is left over after costs.
Two markers show where boats stop arriving if fishing is free for all, and where a single owner would stop.

explore.prompt: Play owner, then play regulator. First find an owner's best fleet when boats are cheaper to run. Then keep the ground open to everyone and use a charge to make newcomers stop where an owner would.

goals.text: Make boats cheaper to run than at the start, then put out the fleet that leaves the most value over after running costs.
hints: Lower the running cost first, then think about where an owner would stop adding boats.
The value left over is the gap between the catch curve and the cost line. Look for where the gap is widest, not where the lines cross.
With cheaper boats the best fleet grows a little. Look between 30 and 50 boats, where one more boat adds only about what it costs.

goals.text: Keep the ground open to everyone, but add a charge per boat so the free-for-all stops at exactly the fleet a single owner would run.
hints: A charge raises what each newcomer must catch before joining is worth it.
Slide the charge up and watch the free-for-all marker move toward the owner's marker.
The right charge is smaller than the profit per boat you saw with a small fleet. It lies between 2 and 4.

feedback.correct: Yes. Under free access, any profit above the running cost works like an open invitation. A higher fish price draws in more boats until the catch per boat again just covers the cost, so the leftover value is drained back to zero.
feedback.incorrect: You probably pictured the same fleet catching more valuable fish. But nobody can keep newcomers out. Extra profit pulls in extra boats, and they stop only when joining no longer pays, which is exactly where nothing is left over.

steps.say: Start with 10 boats. Each catches 9 on average and costs 4 to run, so every boat makes a fat profit. Together they keep 50 after costs.
Nobody owns this ground. It is a common-property resource with open access: anyone may fish, free. Profit draws newcomers. At 30 boats each still catches 7, well above its cost of 4.

So more boats come. At 45 boats each still beats its cost, so joining still pays. But the total left over has fallen from 90 to 67.5. Each newcomer takes fish the other boats would have caught, and it never pays for that.

At 60 boats the catch per boat is exactly 4, the cost of one boat. Now joining no longer pays, so the fleet stops growing, right where the catch curve meets the cost line. The value left over, called the resource rent, is zero.

Now picture one owner. They add a boat only if it adds more catch than it costs, so they stop where curve and line are farthest apart: 30 boats, keeping 90. The extra 30 boats of the free-for-all add 30 to the catch but cost 120.

Make boats cheaper to run and it gets worse. The free-for-all now runs to 80 boats, past the top of the catch curve. Those 80 boats catch only 160, less than the 240 that the owner's 40 boats would catch.

A charge per boat can do the owner's job. Back at a cost of 4, a charge of 1.5 means newcomers must cover 5.5. The dashed line meets the catch curve sooner, so the free-for-all stops at 45: closer to the owner's 30, not there yet.

understand.explanation: When nobody owns a fishing ground, nobody can turn a newcomer away. A new boat joins as long as its own catch beats its running cost, but it never pays for the fish it takes from the other boats. So boats keep coming until the catch per boat just covers the cost, and the resource rent the ground could yield is spent on extra boats. A single owner would stop where one more boat adds only what it costs, and a charge per boat can make newcomers stop in the same place. Banzhaf shows that the 1960s pioneers of pollution pricing, Kneese, Crocker and Dales, kept citing Scott Gordon's 1954 fishery paper, and that they treated rivers and air as shared resources of exactly this kind. The curve here is a simplified version of Gordon's argument, not data from Banzhaf's paper.
understand.quote: Both recognized the wisdom in the popular aphorism that "everybody's property is nobody's property," but demonstrated formally how under open access competition would deplete the value of resources.
understand.quote_where: Section 5, 'Property Rights and Land Tenancy' (on Gordon 1954 and Scott 1955)

connect.caption: This is the model's rule; Banzhaf's history paper gives no equation. N is the number of boats. Under free access, boats join until the average catch per boat equals the running cost c (orange) plus any charge t (green). An owner instead stops where the extra catch from one more boat equals c. For a hump-shaped catch curve, the owner's point always comes before the free-for-all point.

concepts.recap: Free access drains a shared resource's value as users pile in; ownership, or a price on access, stops them where the value is greatest.

activities.prompt: The same fishing ground under three rules. For each, compare where the fleet stops and how much value is left over after running costs.

cases.label: Free for all: 60 boats, nothing left over
One owner: 30 boats, 90 left over as the owner's profit
Open to all, charge per boat: 30 boats, 90 left over, collected as charges

activities.takeaway: The owner and a well-set charge end in the same place: 30 boats and 90 left over. What differs is who keeps the 90. The owner keeps it as profit, or whoever collects the charge does (3 × 30 = 90). So pricing access mimics ownership for things nobody can easily own, like a river or the air. Banzhaf reports that Kneese argued in just these terms for publicly set prices on the use of common property. In practice the right charge is hard to know, because nobody sees the catch curve exactly.

concepts.title: One price finds the cheapest clean-up
concepts.idea: Under a single charge per ton, each firm cuts pollution until its cost of the next cut equals the charge, so firms that can cut cheaply cut more and the total clean-up costs less than equal cuts would.

predict.question: A third factory, C, joins the city. Its clean-up gets pricier even more slowly than Firm A's. The charge stays at $20 a ton. What happens?
options: C cuts the most, and stops where its next ton costs $20, the same as A and B
All three cut the same amount, because they all face the same charge
C cuts nothing: A already cuts cheaply, so C isn't needed
A and B each cut more than before, to keep up with C
why: Right. Each firm compares its own next-ton cost with the charge. C's tons stay cheap for longer, so C keeps cutting further before its next ton reaches $20.
The same charge does not mean the same cut. It means the same next-ton cost, and a firm with cheaper clean-up reaches $20 only after cutting more tons.
No firm waits for the others. Any ton C can cut for less than $20 is cheaper than paying the charge on it, so C cuts those tons.
A's and B's choices depend only on their own costs and the charge. Neither changed, so A still cuts 10 tons and B still cuts 2.5.

terms.means: Cutting pollution: each ton a firm stops releasing is a ton abated
What it costs a firm to cut one more ton of pollution, given how much it has already cut
The 1960s name for a fee a polluter pays on each ton of waste it releases, today often called a pollution tax
Reaching a given amount of clean-up for the smallest possible total cost; also called cost-effective

model.title: Two factories, one charge per ton: who cuts how much, and what it costs
model.note: Teaching model: two firms, each releasing 20 tons. For each firm, the cost of cutting one more ton rises in a straight line as it cuts more. Real clean-up costs are lumpier. Where pollution lands also matters, which is why Kneese wanted charges to differ from place to place. Here a ton counts the same wherever it comes from. Numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data.

Firm B: how much dearer each extra ton cut gets

Firm B: cost of its next ton

steps.say: Two factories each release 20 tons of smoke a year. These bars show how many tons each one cuts.
This slider is a charge. Every ton a factory still releases costs it this much.
These two sliders set how fast cutting gets pricier. Firm A cuts cheaply. For Firm B, each extra ton gets dear quickly.
The third bar is a different plan. Both firms must cut the same amount, adding up to the same total.
Down here are the total bills under each plan.

explore.prompt: Play with the firms' costs and the charge. Watch who cuts, and watch the gap between the two bills.

goals.text: Under the charge, make Firm B cut more tons than Firm A
hints: What decides how far a firm cuts before it stops?
A firm stops when its next ton costs as much as the charge. The firm whose costs climb more slowly gets further first.
Right now Firm A is the cheap cutter. Give that role to Firm B instead.

goals.text: Make the one-charge plan save more than $150 compared with equal cuts
hints: Where does the saving come from? Think about what the equal-cuts rule forces the dear firm to do.
The saving grows when the firms differ more, and when more total cutting is done. You can change either.
Raising the charge alone can do it, but a small step won't be enough.

feedback.correct: Yes. A charge does not hand out equal cuts. It gives every firm the same price for its next ton. The firm with the cheapest clean-up, here C, does the most cutting. A and B are unaffected because their own costs and the charge have not changed.
feedback.incorrect: It is easy to think one charge means one cut for all, or that firms react to each other. Each firm only compares the cost of its own next ton with the charge, and it keeps cutting while cutting is cheaper. A firm with cheap clean-up therefore cuts the most, and every firm ends up at the same next-ton cost.

steps.say: With no charge, cutting only costs money and saves nothing, so neither firm cuts a single ton.
Now charge $10 a ton. Firm A's first cuts cost far less than $10, so it cuts. Economists call cutting pollution abatement, and a fee per ton released was called an effluent charge in the 1960s.
Firm A stops at 5 tons and Firm B at 1.25 tons. Look at the cost of each firm's next ton: both are $10, exactly the charge. That next-ton cost is the marginal abatement cost.
Double the charge to $20. Both firms cut more and stop where their next ton costs $20. Firm A cuts 10 tons and Firm B cuts 2.5.
Now the equal-cuts plan: the same 12.5 tons, split 6.25 each. Firm B is pushed into tons costing it up to $50 each, while Firm A stops at tons costing only $12.50.
Compare the bills: $125 under the charge, about $195 under equal cuts. The air is just as clean, and it costs $70 less. The charge reaches this total in the least-cost way.
Make the firms identical. Now they cut the same under the charge, and the saving disappears. The gain comes entirely from the firms being different.
Now make Firm B's clean-up even dearer than at the start. B cuts just 2 tons, A still cuts 10, and the charge saves $96 over equal cuts.

understand.explanation: Facing one charge per ton, each firm keeps cutting while its next ton is cheaper to cut than to pay for. It stops where that next-ton cost equals the charge. So every firm ends at the same next-ton cost, and firms with cheap clean-up do most of the cutting. Any other split of the same total, such as equal cuts, would make some firm pay more for a ton than another firm would have to, so the charge's split is the least-cost one. Allen Kneese made this argument for effluent charges in the 1960s, and in 1971 Baumol and Oates proved it formally. The paper stresses two points: this finds the cheapest way to reach a chosen target, not whether the target itself is right, and the regulator does not need to know each firm's costs, because each firm works out its own response to the price.
understand.quote: Baumol and Oates provided a formal proof of Kneese's argument that an effluent fee could induce the least-cost method for meeting an arbitrary environmental objective, even if it was not optimal in the sense of equating marginal costs to marginal damages

connect.caption: This is the model's rule; the paper states the argument in words, not as an equation. q_{A} and q_{B} are the tons each firm cuts. Firm A's next ton costs a·q_{A} (slider a) and Firm B's costs b·q_{B} (slider b). Under the charge t, both equal t, so the firm with the smaller cost rise cuts more tons. This holds until a firm has cut all 20 of its tons.

concepts.recap: One price per ton makes every firm stop at the same next-ton cost, so the cheap cutters do the most and the total clean-up costs less than equal cuts.

activities.title: Adding up the two bills

steps.text: Firm A's next ton gets $2 dearer for every ton it cuts. Firm B's gets $8 dearer. So the cost of cutting q tons is the average next-ton cost (half the last ton's cost) times q.
One charge of $20. Firm A cuts until its next ton costs $20, which is at 10 tons. The average ton cost $10, so the bill is 10 × $10.
Firm B reaches $20 a ton after 2.5 tons. The average ton cost $10, so the bill is 2.5 × $10.
Under the charge, 12.5 tons are cut in total for $100 + $25.
Equal cuts of the same 12.5 tons means 6.25 each. Firm A's last ton costs $12.50, an average of $6.25, so its bill is 6.25 × $6.25.
Firm B's last ton costs $50, an average of $25, so its bill is 6.25 × $25.
Equal cuts cost about $39 + $156 = $195, against $125 under the charge.

activities.takeaway: Under equal cuts, B's last ton costs $50 while A could have cut another ton for about $12.50. Shifting tons to the cheap cutter until their next-ton costs match is exactly what the single charge does.

concepts.title: Fix the price or fix the amount
concepts.idea: A pollution charge fixes the price and lets firms decide how much they pollute, while tradable permits fix the amount and let the market decide the price; when clean-up costs are uncertain, only one of the two is known in advance.

predict.question: A lake's fish die if more than 60 tons of waste flow into it in a year. Engineers are unsure what clean-up will really cost. Which tool guarantees that no more than 60 tons go in?
options: A $40-per-ton charge, chosen to hit 60 tons on the engineers' forecast
Permits for 60 tons in total, which firms can buy and sell
Either one: both were tuned to the same forecast
Neither: with uncertain costs, nothing can be guaranteed
why: The charge looks safe because it hits 60 tons on the forecast. But if clean-up costs more than forecast, firms pay the charge and release more than 60 tons, and the fish die.
Right. An enforced limit fixes the tons. Cost surprises move the permit price instead. The price could be high, but the lake gets at most 60 tons.
They do agree when the forecast is right. The lake case turns on what happens when the forecast is wrong, and then only the fixed number stays put.
Something is guaranteed: whichever number you fix. An enforced limit fixes the tons. What it cannot promise is the price firms will end up paying.

terms.means: A system where the government sets a total limit (the cap) on tons of pollution, issues that many permits, and lets firms buy and sell them
The 1960s name, used by Allen Kneese, for a fee paid on each ton of waste released; today it is often called a pollution tax
The mirror relationship between the two tools: fix the price and the market sets the amount, or fix the amount and the market sets the price

model.title: Same forecast, two tools: what moves when clean-up costs surprise us
model.note: Teaching model: firms release 100 tons with no policy. The cost of cutting one more ton rises in a straight line as cuts deepen. Firms know their real costs; the government only has a forecast. The charge and the permit limit start tuned to give the same result on that forecast. The model leaves out where pollution lands (Crocker's location-based trading), Kneese's trial-and-error adjustment of charges, and whether permits are auctioned or given away. Numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data. The paper is a history of ideas and reports no such figures.

controls.label: How costly clean-up really is (× forecast)

outputs.label: Price per ton under the charge ($)

y.label: Cost of cutting one more ton ($)

series.label: Forecast cost of the next cut
Real cost of the next cut

steps.say: This solid line shows what it costs to cut one more ton of pollution. Move left and you have cut more, so each extra ton gets dearer.
The dashed line is the engineers' forecast. This slider sets how far reality lands from it. Watch the solid line tilt.
The flat line is a charge per ton. Firms keep cutting while a cut is cheaper than paying the charge.
The upright line is a limit: only that many tons are allowed, as permits that firms can buy and sell.
These boxes read out the pollution and the price per ton under each tool.

explore.prompt: Play the regulator who got the forecast wrong. Steer each tool after a cost surprise and notice which number you have to give up.

goals.text: Suppose clean-up turns out to cost double the forecast. Change the charge so that pollution under the charge is held to 60 tons again.
hints: Set the surprise first, then ask what charge the steeper cost line would need to meet at 60 tons.
The charge outcome sits where the flat charge line crosses the solid cost line. Drag the charge until that crossing is back at 60 tons.
When the cost line gets twice as steep, the cost of the 60th-ton cut grows by that same factor, so the charge has to grow by it too.

goals.text: Clean-up costs are still double the forecast. Now use the permit limit instead: move it until the permit price is back to $40, the price the charge had fixed.
hints: You don't set the permit price. The market does. So which control can bring it down?
The permit price is the height of the solid cost line at the limit. Move the limit to where that line is lower.
On the doubled line, the cost falls as you move right toward 100 tons, so the limit lands somewhere between 60 and 100.

feedback.correct: Yes. Only an enforced limit on tons fixes the amount. When clean-up costs surprise us, the permit price absorbs the surprise and the lake still gets at most 60 tons.
feedback.incorrect: You may have assumed that a charge tuned to 60 tons will deliver 60 tons. That only holds if the cost forecast is right. A charge fixes the price, so a cost surprise shows up as more or less pollution. A limit fixes the tons, so the surprise shows up in the permit price.

steps.say: Start with costs exactly as forecast. The $40 charge and the 60-ton limit were chosen to land in the same place: 60 tons released, $40 per ton.
Now clean-up turns out 50% dearer. Under the charge, firms stop cutting sooner, because paying $40 beats a costlier cut. Pollution rises to about 73 tons, and the price is still $40.

Under the limit, pollution can't rise: it stays at 60 tons. Instead, cutting costs more, so firms bid more for permits and the price climbs to $60. A fixed total of tradable permits like this is called cap-and-trade.
Flip it: clean-up is cheaper than feared. The same charge now buys extra clean-up, down to about 33 tons. The permit price falls to $24 while pollution sits at 60 tons.
In the 1960s Allen Kneese called a fee on each ton of waste an effluent charge. Whichever number you fix, the market sets the other. That mirror is the price–quantity duality.

A big surprise makes the trade-off plain. The charge keeps its $40 but lets about 78 tons through. The cap keeps 60 tons, but its price jumps to $72. With uncertain costs you can know one number in advance, never both.

understand.explanation: A charge and a permit limit both put a price on pollution, and they are mirror images. With a charge, the government names the price per ton and firms choose how much to cut, so the amount of pollution depends on what clean-up really costs. With tradable permits, the government names the total tons and firms trade the permits, so the price depends on those same costs. If the cost forecast is right the two tools land in the same place; if it is wrong, the number that wasn't fixed moves. The paper traces this pair from Kneese's effluent charges (1964) to the permit proposals of Crocker (1966) and Dales (1968). Dales argued that permits give more certainty over environmental quality, because a charge needs trial and error to find the right price. Which tool is better overall is still debated, and this teaching model leaves out issues such as where the pollution lands.
understand.quote: Whereas effluent charges or pollution taxes set a price on pollution, allowing the market to determine the quantity demanded at that price, tradable permits set an upper bound on the quantity of pollution, allowing the market to determine the price at that quantity supplied.
understand.quote_where: Section 4, Pollution Permits: Thomas Crocker and John Dales

check.task: Leave the charge at $40 and the limit at 60 tons. Put the model in a state where the charge lets through at least 10 tons more pollution than the permits do.
check.hint: With the charge and the limit locked, only the cost surprise is left. Which way must it go for firms facing a fixed charge to stop cutting sooner?
check.misconception: That a charge locks in the amount of pollution, or that dearer clean-up makes firms cut more. Under a fixed charge, dearer clean-up means firms pay the charge rather than cut, so pollution rises above the limit's level.

connect.caption: These are the model's own rules; the paper, a history of ideas, gives no equation. The orange parts belong to the charge: you fix the price, and the pollution is worked out. The green parts belong to the permits: you fix the tons, and the price is worked out. The surprise term (blue) appears in the worked-out number each time, which is the duality the paper describes between Kneese's prices and Crocker and Dales's tradable quotas.

concepts.recap: A charge fixes the price and lets pollution float; a cap fixes the pollution and lets the price float. When clean-up costs surprise us, only the number we fixed is known in advance.

activities.prompt: Same $40 charge, same 60-ton limit, three different realities. Watch which number moves under each tool.
activities.takeaway: Across the three cases, the charge's price never changes but its pollution swings from about 33 to 75 tons. The permits' pollution never changes but their price swings from $24 to $64. The surprise lands on whichever number you didn't fix.

concepts.title: The tax that got Pigou's name later
concepts.idea: The citation record and the pioneers' own arguments show that 1960s pollution pricing grew from common-property and resource-development thinking, and the 'Pigouvian' label was applied to it around 1970.

terms.means: A fee a firm pays for each ton of waste it dumps into a river or the air. This was the 1960s name for what we now call a pollution tax.
Something anyone can use and nobody owns, such as a fishery, groundwater or the air. Each user takes too much because the loss is shared by everyone.

concepts.recap: Pollution pricing grew mostly from American ideas about overused shared resources; Pigou's name was added around 1970. That is one historian's documented reading, not settled fact.

understand.explanation: Earlier in this lesson, the tax on pollution was presented as Pigou's idea. Arthur Pigou, a Cambridge economist writing in the 1920s and 1930s, argued that a tax could close the gap between private and social cost. In the 1960s, American economists proposed two tools. Allen Kneese proposed an effluent charge: a fee on each ton of waste a firm dumps into a river. Thomas Crocker and John Dales proposed tradable pollution rights. The historian H. Spencer Banzhaf checked whom these pioneers actually cited, and they almost never mentioned Pigou. Instead they drew on work about the common property resource, something anyone can use and nobody owns, such as a fishery, groundwater or the air, which each user therefore overuses. The label 'Pigouvian tax' only spread after about 1970. Banzhaf does not deny that Pigou mattered. His account is an interpretation, set out in a working paper that was not peer-reviewed. Citation counts show who was cited, not every idea that was in the air.
understand.quote: This paper has argued that the early literature on pollution pricing was rooted in questions about common property resources and the increasing returns from developing natural resources. Both topics were treated by broad literatures by the 1960s, including distinctly American traditions not particularly associated with Pigou.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened, earliest first. Use what you just read: Pigou wrote first, the 1960s pioneers came next, and the label arrived last.
items: Pigou's The Economics of Welfare describes factory smoke as an uncharged loss to the community (1920; 4th edition 1932)
Scott Gordon shows how open access drains the value of a fishery (1954)
Buchanan and Stubblebine use the term 'Pigouvian tax', its first appearance on JSTOR (1962)
Allen Kneese proposes 'effluent charges' on waste dumped into rivers (1964)
Crocker (1966) and Dales (1968) propose tradable pollution rights, citing Gordon but not Pigou
Baumol and Oates describe Kneese's work as part of a 'Pigouvian tradition' (1971)
Baumol and Oates's textbook The Theory of Environmental Policy helps enshrine the Pigouvian framing (1975)
hints: Pigou's book comes first and the textbook label comes last.
Gordon's fishery paper came before all the 1960s pollution proposals.
The phrase 'Pigouvian tax' existed by 1962, but it was only attached to Kneese's charges around 1971.
activities.explanation: The order matters for the argument. Pigou wrote in the 1920s and 1930s. About three decades passed before the pollution proposals of 1964 to 1968, and those proposals cited Gordon's work on common property rather than Pigou. The term 'Pigouvian tax' was available from 1962 but rare. It was only attached to Kneese's effluent charges around 1971, by Baumol and Oates. The name came after the work, not before it.

activities.prompt: Step through Banzhaf's evidence one piece at a time. At each stage, ask: does this fit the story that pollution taxes were built straight from Pigou?

stages.label: 1. The textbook story
stages.text: Encyclopedias tell a straight line: Pigou developed the idea, and a 'Pigouvian tax' applies it to pollution. Banzhaf calls this the conventional narrative, in which 1960s economists 'picked up where A.C. Pigou had left off some 30 years before'.

stages.label: 2. A 30-year silence
stages.text: Pigou's examples closest to pollution, such as smoking chimneys, were 'the group most ignored in the literature until at least the late 1950s'. Baumol (1952) called such cases 'freakish exceptions'. If the idea passed straight down from Pigou, it is odd that almost no one used it for three decades.

stages.label: 3. The pioneers' own books
stages.text: Kneese, the leading figure in pollution pricing, called his fees 'effluent charges'. After a 1960 mention of Pigou's general welfare economics, he did not cite Pigou at all until the end of the decade. On JSTOR, the term 'Pigouvian tax' first appears in 1962 and turns up only 12 times in the whole of the 1960s.

stages.label: 4. Two conversations that rarely met
stages.text: A Google Scholar search for 1962 to 1972 found 65 works mentioning both Kneese and Pigou, 982 mentioning Kneese without Pigou, and 2,110 mentioning Pigou without Kneese. Pigou was widely known. He just was not part of the pollution-charge conversation.

stages.label: 5. What they cited instead
stages.text: Crocker and Dales make 'absolutely no reference' to Pigou. Both cite Gordon's (1954) analysis of the fishery as a common property resource. Crocker compared rights to air with an old groundwater rule that let each owner pump out a shared reservoir. By 1971, Kneese himself called his approach 'the management of common property resources approach'.

stages.label: 6. The label arrives
stages.text: In 1971 Baumol and Oates proved Kneese's point formally and described his work as part of a 'Pigouvian tradition'. After that, references to Pigou rose fast, and by the late 1970s the framing was in textbooks. Banzhaf calls this a reinterpretation of work that had already been developed separately.

activities.takeaway: Put together, the stages tell a different story. The 'Pigouvian tax' on pollution was mostly not built from Pigou. Its 1960s inventors barely cited him and borrowed instead from American ideas about overused shared resources like fisheries and groundwater. Pigou's name was attached to their work later.

activities.prompt: Historians agree on the silence and the late label. They differ on what explains them. Compare three explanations.

cases.label: 'Grafted on' (Medema 2020a)
cases.text: The line from Pigou was broken and later reconnected. His ideas were refined into today's concept of externalities without much real-world use. When environmental problems loomed larger, this revised theory was 'grafted into' the new field of environmental economics. On this view, nothing much filled the gap.

cases.label: 'Oral tradition'
cases.text: Pigou's idea was so taken for granted that no one bothered to cite it. Some support: Kneese wrote in 1964 that 'Economists have long held that technological spillovers can be counteracted by levying taxes'. On this view, the silence hides Pigou's influence rather than showing its absence.

cases.label: American roots (Banzhaf 2020)
cases.text: There was a continuous tradition, but it ran back to American land and resource economics, not to Pigou. It covered open-access commons like fisheries and groundwater, tenant farmers wearing out land, and the gains from developing rivers at scale. The pioneers were trained in this tradition and cited it. Pigou's name was added around 1970.

activities.takeaway: All three accounts accept the citation gap. The oral-tradition reading can explain the silence about Pigou. But Banzhaf points out that silence is only negative evidence, and the pioneers also gave positive evidence of other roots: their citations to Gordon and their analogies to groundwater and land tenancy. Banzhaf still calls Pigou 'undeniably an important source', just 'one of many'.

activities.question: From 1962 to 1972: 65 works mention both Kneese and Pigou, 982 mention Kneese without Pigou, and 2,110 mention Pigou without Kneese. What do these counts on their own support?

options.text: Pigou was little known to economists in the 1960s.
options.feedback: No. Over 2,000 works mentioned Pigou, so he was widely cited. The point is that those works rarely overlapped with the work on pollution charges.

options.text: The literature on pollution charges and the literature citing Pigou were mostly separate conversations.
options.feedback: Yes. Very few works mention both, so the two bodies of writing rarely met. Banzhaf concludes they 'were operating in quite distinct spheres'. Counts show who was cited, though, not every idea people carried in their heads.

options.text: Kneese took his idea from Pigou without crediting him.
options.feedback: The counts cannot show that. Missing citations are consistent with copying, with an unspoken tradition, or with other sources. Banzhaf uses the pioneers' positive citations, for example to Gordon, to argue for other sources.

hints: Compare the size of the overlap with the two separate groups.
65 is tiny next to 982 and 2,110.

activities.question: Weighing all the evidence, which account of where pollution pricing came from do you find best supported? There is no single graded answer. Read the feedback on your choice and on the others.

options.text: It grew mainly from American thinking about shared resources and resource development, and Pigou's name was added around 1970.
options.feedback: This is Banzhaf's reading. It fits both the silence and the positive evidence: the citations to Gordon's fishery, Crocker's groundwater analogy, and Kneese's own 1971 'common property resources approach'. Its limits: it is one historian's account in a working paper that was not peer-reviewed, and it does not claim Pigou was irrelevant.

options.text: Pigou's idea was so standard that no one needed to cite it.
options.feedback: The oral-tradition reading explains why Pigou is missing, and Kneese's remark that economists had 'long held' such views gives it some support. It struggles to explain why the pioneers framed their work around commons and property rights and cited Gordon and Coase rather than Pigou.

options.text: The Pigou line was lost for decades, then his revised theory was grafted onto the new field.
options.feedback: Medema's reading agrees with Banzhaf on the gap and the late label. It differs on whether another tradition was flowing during the gap. The pioneers' training in agricultural and resource economics is the evidence Banzhaf uses to say that one was.

options.text: Pigou invented the pollution tax, and the 1960s economists simply applied his work.
options.feedback: This is the conventional story, and it is the one the evidence most strains. The leading 1960s texts barely cite Pigou, and the 'Pigouvian' label only spread after about 1970. Pigou did argue for correcting taxes, but treating the 1960s proposals as direct applications of his work does not match the citation record.
